To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) Russian vowel reduction is a complex phenomenon, and (2) the Optimality-Theoretics framework is a very good tool for modeling the patterns of Russian vowel reduction.

(i) the Russian reduction patterns can be unified in a non-unitary OT analysis; (ii) this unified account can be extended to include the so-called "dissimulative" patterns, which have traditionally been considered a separate type of reduction, and (iii) this unified account of the Russian reduction patterns does not rely on featural dissimilative constraints, but instead relies on a number of other, more traditional, constraints, including those on sonority and lengthening under

(i) the standard Russian vowel reduction system is best analyzed as involving two patterns, and that (ii) the "dissimilation" pattern seen in the dialects of Russian is best analyzed as an effect of constraints on sonorant consonants and on the length of stressed vowels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) What is the phonological nature of vowel reduction?;

the following questions: (i) what is the nature of the constraints responsible for vowel reduction in Russian, (ii) what is the role of the sonority hierarchy in the reduction process, (iii) how do we capture dialectal patterns in which the quality of the unstressed vowel is determined by the quality of the preceding stressed vowel, (iv) what is the status of the so-called “dissimilation” constraint in the analysis of vowel reduction in Russian dialects?
the following questions: (1) What are the phonetic properties of vowel reduction in Standard Russian?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the analysis of vowel reduction in Russian presented here is a unified account of standard, dialectal, and “dissimilativ” patterns.
the analysis presented here provides an elegant and unified account of the reduction patterns seen in Russian.

Optimality Theory, with its emphasis on the interplay of multiple constraints in a single grammar, is an extremely promising approach to the analysis of complex phonological patterns such as those found in Russian.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the patterns of vowel reduction found in Russian dialects and in Standard Russian can all be accounted for in a single, unified analysis.
the analysis presented here provides a unified account of vowel reduction in Russian that is both theoretically and empirically motivated.
we have shown that a unified account of vowel reduction in Russian can be given, one that is able to handle standard, dialectal, and "dissimilitative" reduction patterns.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a unified approach to Russian vowel reduction patterns, including dialectal and dissimilative ones, can be developed within OT, and that this analysis is more economical than previous accounts of these patterns.
a unified account of vowel reduction in Russian is possible within the OT framework, even when a number of different dialectal patterns are taken into consideration.
a single set of Optimality-Theoretically motivated constraints can account for a wide range of reduction patterns in Russian.
